exploration.title: Castle Design Lab
exploration.subject: History
exploration.summary: Test how a gate, ditch and projecting tower change routes and wall-side views.
exploration.question: How did separate defenses change an approach to a stone castle?
exploration.explanation: This 13th-century English-inspired composite is not a reconstruction of one castle. Gatehouses controlled passage, ditches interrupted approaches, projecting towers changed viewing positions along wall faces, and multiple wall lines could add successive barriers. Castles also housed households, workers and administrators. Designs varied by period, site, terrain and resources; this controlled model compares routes and illustrated viewing directions, not weapon ranges or the outcome of a siege.

experiments.title: Compare two open-gate routes
experiments.instruction: Keep the gate open and ditch at 22 m. Predict which routes reach an entrance, compare the bridge route with the north-wall route, then inspect both endpoints.
experiments.observe: The bridge reaches the entrance; the north route stops at the ditch. Explain why opening one gate does not remove a ditch or create a doorway through another wall.

experiments.title: Compare wall-side viewpoints
experiments.instruction: Keep the bridge route, closed gate and 22 m ditch fixed. Predict which position shows more adjoining wall faces, then compare the flat corner with the projecting tower.
experiments.observe: Count the dashed viewing directions in both trials. Explain why projecting beyond a wall changes what can be seen; the lines are illustrative directions, not complete visibility or weapon ranges.

exploration.misconception: No single feature made a castle impregnable. Not every castle had stone walls, a keep, concentric defenses or a water-filled moat; ditches could be dry, and designs changed over centuries.
